paper_context.research_question: How can a novel fusion learning architecture based on word embeddings improve the automatic discovery of hypernym-hyponym relations for semantic hierarchy construction?
main_claims: The proposed fusion learning architecture, combining discriminative (RNN) and generative (MLP) models with a simple lexical structure rule, effectively learns semantic hierarchies via word embeddings.
This architecture achieves an F1-score of 74.20% and a precision of 91.60% on a manually labeled test dataset, outperforming state-of-the-art methods for hypernym-hyponym relation discovery.
Combining the fusion learning architecture with manually-built hierarchies (Wikipedia and CilinE) further improves the F1-score to 82.01%.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript presents a novel fusion learning architecture for automatic hypernym-hyponym relation discovery, combining discriminative (RNN) and generative (MLP) neural networks with a simple lexical structure rule. The logical flow is clear, moving from problem identification (limitations of manual and existing automatic methods) to a proposed solution, detailed architectural components, experimental setup, and comprehensive evaluation against state-of-the-art methods. The paper effectively demonstrates empirical improvements in F1-score and precision on a Chinese test dataset, including out-of-domain data, and shows the complementarity of the method with manually-built hierarchies. While the core argument for the fusion architecture's effectiveness is well-supported by experimental results, some claims, particularly regarding language independence, lack empirical validation. The contribution of the lexical rule, despite its high precision, is also shown to be limited in scope and its synergy with the neural components could be more deeply analyzed.
logical_argument_graph: Problem Identification: Manual semantic hierarchy construction is labor-intensive and limited. Automatic hypernym-hyponym discovery is crucial but challenging due to limitations of existing methods (pattern-based, distributional, web mining, shallow word embedding methods).

Proposed Solution: A novel 'fusion learning architecture' for semantic hierarchy construction, combining strengths of discriminative (RNN) and generative (MLP) models, enhanced by a 'simple lexical structure rule' for specific linguistic phenomena (Chinese compound nouns), all built upon word embeddings (Skip-gram).

Architectural Components & Fusion: Details the use of Skip-gram embeddings, MLP for the generative model (aiming for high precision), RNN for the discriminative model (aiming for high recall), a Boolean 'AND' operator for fusing MLP and RNN outputs (MMLP+RNN) to balance precision/recall, and a lexical structure rule (MlexicalRule) for Chinese compound nouns (aiming for 100% precision for a subset). The final MFusion combines MMLP+RNN with MlexicalRule.

Experimental Setup: Describes the use of Baidubaike for word embedding training, CilinE for training hypernym-hyponym relations, and a manually labeled test set (from Fu et al., 2014) for evaluation. Metrics include Precision, Recall, and F1-score. Details parameter settings and training procedures for the neural networks.

Evaluation & Results: Presents a component-wise analysis, demonstrating that MMLP+RNN achieves higher precision than individual components. Shows that MFusion achieves state-of-the-art F1 (74.20%) and high precision (91.60%) on the main test set, outperforming previous methods like MEmb. Further demonstrates MFusion's state-of-the-art F1 (57.53%) and improved precision (79.92%) on out-of-CilinE data. Illustrates that combining MFusion with manually-built hierarchies (Wikipedia, CilinE) further boosts F1 to 82.01% via transitivity inference.

Conclusion & Generalization: Concludes that the proposed method is novel, achieves state-of-the-art performance, is complementary with manual resources, and claims the architecture is language-independent and easily adaptable to other languages.

concerns.title: Limited Scope and Impact of Lexical Rule
concerns.description: The simple lexical structure rule, while achieving 100% precision for Chinese compound nouns, has a very low recall (16.88%), indicating its applicability is limited to a small subset of hypernym-hyponym relations. The paper states it 'only takes effect for CNs which are minority.' Furthermore, the experiment (Table 4) showing MEmb+lexicalRule not improving F1 over MEmb suggests that the neural components might already capture these specific cases, making the rule's incremental contribution to the overall fusion model's performance less clear or redundant for general cases.

concerns.title: Limited Justification for Boolean 'AND' Fusion Strategy
concerns.description: The paper fuses the generative and discriminative architectures using a simple Boolean 'AND' operator. While this is stated to achieve higher precision, the rationale for choosing this specific, rigid fusion strategy over other potential methods (e.g., weighted combination of scores, learned fusion layers, soft voting) is not thoroughly explored or justified. This raises questions about whether the chosen fusion is optimal for balancing precision and recall, or if a more sophisticated approach could yield better overall performance.

concerns.actionable_suggestion: Discuss alternative fusion strategies and provide a brief justification for why the Boolean 'AND' was chosen (e.g., simplicity, interpretability, or specific precision goals). concerns.title: Superficial Depth of Failure Analysis
concerns.description: The paper provides an example of a failure case (e.g., '乌头属' and '毛茛科') where the MFusion method fails to learn the semantic hierarchy. The explanation attributes this to 'semantic similarity effects representations close to each other in the embedding space.' While plausible, this explanation is high-level. A deeper analysis of *why* the model struggles with these specific types of relations, what characteristics make them challenging, and how the model could be made more robust would strengthen the paper. The reliance on external manually-built hierarchies to 'fix' these cases, while effective, highlights a limitation of the core learning architecture that could be further investigated.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes a novel fusion learning architecture (MFusion) for automatic hypernym-hyponym relation discovery, aiming to construct semantic hierarchies. The architecture combines a generative model (MLP), a discriminative model (RNN), and a simple lexical structure rule, all leveraging word embeddings. The core reasoning is that this fusion, by combining different model strengths and linguistic cues, can achieve superior performance, particularly high precision, and is generalizable. The evaluation demonstrates state-of-the-art F1-score and high precision on a Chinese test dataset, improved performance on out-of-CilinE data, and complementarity with manually-built hierarchies. Methodologically, the use of established neural components and word embeddings is sound, and the evaluation setup is comprehensive. However, key claims like language independence lack empirical validation, and certain architectural choices, such as the Boolean 'AND' fusion, are not fully justified as optimal, potentially limiting overall performance or generalizability.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript addresses the challenge of automatic hypernym-hyponym relation discovery for semantic hierarchy construction. It proposes a novel "fusion learning architecture" that incrementally advances the state-of-the-art by combining established neural network paradigms—specifically, a discriminative Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) and a generative Multilayer Perceptron (MLP)—with a simple, domain-specific lexical structure rule. The core reasoning is that while word embeddings effectively capture semantic relations, individual models (discriminative or generative) often present trade-offs between precision and recall. The proposed fusion strategy, employing a Boolean "AND" operator, aims to leverage the strengths of both (e.g., higher recall from RNN, higher precision from MLP) to achieve a more balanced and superior overall performance. Furthermore, recognizing that purely embedding-based models might overlook explicit lexical structure information, a simple rule tailored for Chinese compound nouns is integrated to capture specific linguistic patterns. This combined architecture, applied to Chinese, demonstrates a notable improvement in F1-score and significantly higher precision compared to prior word embedding-based methods and other traditional approaches (pattern-based, distributional, web mining). The paper also explores the architecture's complementarity with existing manually-built hierarchies and posits its language independence, though this latter claim lacks empirical validation within the manuscript.
logical_argument_graph: The problem of automatic semantic hierarchy construction, particularly hypernym-hyponym relation discovery, is challenging due to the limitations of manual creation and existing automatic methods.

Previous automatic approaches (pattern-based, distributional, web mining, word embedding-based like Fu et al. 2014) suffer from issues such as low recall/precision, reliance on shallow semantics, or requiring advanced clustering.
Word embeddings capture rich semantic relations (Mikolov et al., 2013b), but a single neural model type (discriminative or generative) has inherent trade-offs in precision and recall.
A novel fusion learning architecture is proposed, combining a generative MLP (designed for high precision) and a discriminative RNN (designed for higher recall).
This fusion is achieved by applying a Boolean 'AND' operator to the outputs of the two neural architectures, aiming to combine their complementary strengths.
To address the limitation of word embeddings ignoring explicit lexical structures, a simple lexical structure rule (specific to Chinese compound nouns) is integrated to assist the fusion model.
The proposed MFusion architecture is evaluated on a manually labeled Chinese test dataset and compared against various state-of-the-art methods.
MFusion achieves a new state-of-the-art F1-score and significantly higher precision, demonstrating its effectiveness.
Further experiments show that MFusion also achieves state-of-the-art performance on out-of-CilinE data and is complementary to manually-built hierarchies, further improving performance when combined.
The architecture is claimed to be language-independent and easily adaptable to other languages.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript proposes a novel 'fusion learning architecture' for automatic hypernym-hyponym relation discovery, aiming to construct semantic hierarchies. The core innovation lies in combining a discriminative model (RNN) and a generative model (MLP) using a Boolean 'AND' operator, further augmented by a simple lexical structure rule. This architecture leverages word embeddings to capture semantic information. The paper argues that this fusion balances the strengths of individual components (high precision from generative, higher recall from discriminative, and 100% precision for specific lexical patterns). Empirical results on a Chinese dataset demonstrate state-of-the-art F1-score and significantly high precision (91.60%), outperforming previous methods. The architecture's ability to be combined with manually-built hierarchies for further improvement and its claimed language-independence are also highlighted.

Automatic hypernym-hyponym discovery is the key challenge for semantic hierarchy construction.
Previous automatic methods (pattern-based, distributional, web mining, word embedding-based) have limitations in recall, precision, or semantic depth.
Word embeddings capture semantic relations but often require linear transformations or advanced clustering.
Discriminative models (RNN) offer higher recall but lower precision for classification.
Generative models (MLP) can achieve high precision by adjusting thresholds but often suffer from low recall.
Lexical structure rules, though limited in coverage, can provide very high precision for specific linguistic phenomena (e.g., Chinese compound nouns).

The paper proposes a novel fusion learning architecture (MFusion) for automatic hypernym-hyponym relation discovery, aiming to construct semantic hierarchies. The architecture combines a generative model (MLP), a discriminative model (RNN), and a simple lexical structure rule, all leveraging word embeddings. The core reasoning is that this fusion, by combining different model strengths and linguistic cues, can achieve superior performance, particularly high precision, and is generalizable. The evaluation demonstrates state-of-the-art F1-score and high precision on a Chinese test dataset, improved performance on out-of-CilinE data, and complementarity with manually-built hierarchies. Methodologically, the use of established neural components and word embeddings is sound, and the evaluation setup is comprehensive. However, key claims like language independence lack empirical validation, and certain architectural choices, such as the Boolean 'AND' fusion, are not fully justified as optimal, potentially limiting overall performance or generalizability.

The manuscript addresses the challenge of automatic hypernym-hyponym relation discovery for semantic hierarchy construction. It proposes a novel "fusion learning architecture" that incrementally advances the state-of-the-art by combining established neural network paradigms—specifically, a discriminative Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) and a generative Multilayer Perceptron (MLP)—with a simple, domain-specific lexical structure rule. The core reasoning is that while word embeddings effectively capture semantic relations, individual models (discriminative or generative) often present trade-offs between precision and recall. The proposed fusion strategy, employing a Boolean "AND" operator, aims to leverage the strengths of both (e.g., higher recall from RNN, higher precision from MLP) to achieve a more balanced and superior overall performance. Furthermore, recognizing that purely embedding-based models might overlook explicit lexical structure information, a simple rule tailored for Chinese compound nouns is integrated to capture specific linguistic patterns. This combined architecture, applied to Chinese, demonstrates a notable improvement in F1-score and significantly higher precision compared to prior word embedding-based methods and other traditional approaches (pattern-based, distributional, web mining). The paper also explores the architecture's complementarity with existing manually-built hierarchies and posits its language independence, though this latter claim lacks empirical validation within the manuscript.

The manuscript proposes a novel 'fusion learning architecture' for automatic hypernym-hyponym relation discovery, aiming to construct semantic hierarchies. The core innovation lies in combining a discriminative model (RNN) and a generative model (MLP) using a Boolean 'AND' operator, further augmented by a simple lexical structure rule. This architecture leverages word embeddings to capture semantic information. The paper argues that this fusion balances the strengths of individual components (high precision from generative, higher recall from discriminative, and 100% precision for specific lexical patterns). Empirical results on a Chinese dataset demonstrate state-of-the-art F1-score and significantly high precision (91.60%), outperforming previous methods. The architecture's ability to be combined with manually-built hierarchies for further improvement and its claimed language-independence are also highlighted.
specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper introduces a novel fusion learning architecture (MFusion) for automatic hypernym-hyponym relation discovery, integrating discriminative (RNN) and generative (MLP) models with a simple lexical structure rule. The core reasoning is that this fusion leverages complementary strengths of different model types and linguistic cues to achieve superior performance, particularly high precision, in constructing semantic hierarchies. The empirical results strongly support the claims of achieving state-of-the-art F1-scores (74.20%) and high precision (91.60%) on a manually labeled Chinese test dataset, outperforming various baseline methods. Furthermore, the architecture demonstrates improved performance on out-of-CilinE data (F1=57.53%) and significant gains when combined with manually-built hierarchies (F1=82.01%). While the high precision of the lexical rule (100% for Chinese compound nouns) is verified, its overall impact is limited by low recall. The most significant overstatement is the claim of language independence, which lacks any empirical validation within the manuscript. The choice of a Boolean 'AND' operator for fusion, while effective, is not thoroughly justified as optimal, leaving room for alternative interpretations regarding potential further performance gains.
logical_argument_graph: Manual semantic hierarchy construction is labor-intensive and limited in coverage.
Existing automatic methods for hypernym-hyponym discovery have limitations (e.g., low recall/precision, shallow semantics).
Word embeddings effectively capture semantic relations and can be leveraged for this task (Assumption A1).
Discriminative (RNN) and generative (MLP) models offer complementary strengths (RNN for higher recall, MLP for higher precision).
Lexical structure rules can capture specific linguistic patterns (e.g., Chinese compound nouns) with high precision (Assumption A5).
The proposed solution is a fusion architecture (MFusion) combining RNN, MLP (using a Boolean 'AND' operator, Assumption A6), and a lexical rule.
Hypothesis: This fusion will leverage complementary strengths, achieve higher F1 and precision, and be generalizable.

Experimental setup involves training word embeddings on a large Chinese corpus (Baidubaike, Assumption A2), using CilinE for training hypernym-hyponym relations (Assumption A3), and evaluating on a manually labeled test set with high inter-annotator agreement (Assumption A4) and out-of-CilinE data.
Empirical results demonstrate that MFusion achieves state-of-the-art F1 (74.20%) and high precision (91.60%) on the test set (Claim C2).
The lexical rule component (MlexicalRule) achieves 100% precision for Chinese compound nouns, albeit with low recall (Claim C5).
The fusion of MLP and RNN (MMLP+RNN) achieves higher precision than its individual components (Claim C6).
MFusion achieves a new state-of-the-art F1-score (57.53%) on out-of-CilinE data (Claim C7).
Combining MFusion with manually-built hierarchies (Wikipedia and CilinE) further improves the F1-score to 82.01% (Claim C3).

Conclusion: The proposed method effectively learns semantic hierarchies, outperforms state-of-the-art methods, is complementary with manual hierarchies, and is claimed to be language-independent (Claim C4).

consensus_findings: The proposed fusion learning architecture, combining discriminative (RNN) and generative (MLP) models with a simple lexical structure rule, is a novel architectural contribution for hypernym-hyponym relation discovery.
The MFusion architecture achieves state-of-the-art F1-scores and notably high precision (91.60%) on the main Chinese test dataset, outperforming previous methods.
The method demonstrates improved performance on 'out-of-CilinE' data, achieving a new state-of-the-art F1-score of 57.53% with significant precision improvement.
Combining the MFusion architecture with manually-built hierarchies (Wikipedia and CilinE) further improves the F1-score to 82.01%, indicating complementarity with existing knowledge resources.
The simple lexical structure rule achieves 100% precision for Chinese compound nouns (CNs) but has very low recall (16.88%), indicating its limited scope and applicability to a minority of relations.
disagreements: Reviewers hold differing views on the *nature* of the paper's novelty: one 'novelty_assessor_incremental' reviewer identifies a 'strong incremental contribution', while the 'novelty_assessor_disruptive' reviewer, while acknowledging 'high novelty' from a disruptive lens, also notes 'limited disruptive potential, primarily incremental'. The 'claim_verifier' explicitly states 'incremental' but 'not disruptive'. This indicates a controlled disagreement on whether the work represents a fundamental shift or a significant refinement within existing paradigms.

There is a slight disagreement on the severity of the concern regarding the Boolean 'AND' fusion strategy: 'structure_analyst' and 'methodology_auditor' rate it as 'moderate' severity, while 'novelty_assessor_incremental', 'novelty_assessor_disruptive', and 'claim_verifier' rate it as 'minor' severity.
uncertainty_hotspots: The claim of language-independence (C4) is stated as a feature but is not empirically validated for languages other than Chinese in the manuscript. This is a significant overstatement without supporting evidence, especially given language-specific components like Chinese segmentation and the lexical rule.

The 'simple lexical structure rule' (C5), despite its 100% precision, has very low recall (16.88%), limiting its overall utility and generalizability beyond Chinese compound nouns. Its incremental value when neural models might already capture these relations is also uncertain.

The optimality of the Boolean 'AND' fusion strategy (Assumption A6) is not empirically demonstrated against other fusion methods (e.g., weighted sum, learned fusion layers), raising uncertainty about whether the best possible balance of precision and recall, or a higher F1-score, is achieved.

The term 'state-of-the-art' for claims C2 and C7 is relative to the specific set of baselines chosen for comparison in the paper. While the baselines are diverse, the claim's broader validity against all contemporary methods remains an open question without an exhaustive external review.

The depth of failure analysis is superficial; specific reasons for the model's failure to learn certain semantic hierarchies (e.g., '乌头属' and '毛茛科') are attributed to semantic similarity effects in embedding space, but a systematic analysis or solution is not provided.
model_diversity_effects: The 'structure_analyst' (logical-coherence-first) focused on the clear logical flow and modularity, highlighting the strong empirical performance and generalizability to out-of-domain data as strengths, while identifying the unvalidated language independence and limited lexical rule scope as logical gaps.

The 'methodology_auditor' (reproducibility-and-validity-first) emphasized the novelty of the architecture and high precision as strengths, but critically assessed the lack of empirical validation for language independence, the sub-optimality of the fusion strategy, and the domain dependence on out-of-CilinE data as methodological flaws impacting validity and reproducibility.

The 'novelty_assessor_incremental' (incremental-contribution lens) identified strong incremental contributions in the effective fusion of complementary models, meaningful precision improvement, and synergy with manual hierarchies. Concerns were primarily focused on the limited scope of the lexical rule and the unvalidated nature of language independence, which constrain the overall incremental impact.

The 'novelty_assessor_disruptive' (disruptive-thinking lens) perceived high novelty in the specific fusion architecture, noting its distinct conceptual design and high precision as potentially disruptive. However, the unproven language-independence claim was a major limiting factor for its realized disruptive potential, and the simplicity of the fusion operator was noted as a minor concern.

The 'claim_verifier' (evidence-and-uncertainty-first) rigorously confirmed empirically supported performance claims (C2, C3, C6, C7) but strongly flagged the language independence claim (C4) as unsubstantiated and the lexical rule's impact (C5) as limited. This role also raised uncertainty about the optimality of the Boolean 'AND' fusion strategy and the relativity of 'state-of-the-art' claims.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: The paper introduces a novel fusion learning architecture (MFusion) for automatic hypernym-hyponym relation discovery, combining discriminative (RNN) and generative (MLP) models with a simple lexical structure rule. The architecture leverages word embeddings and demonstrates state-of-the-art F1-scores and notably high precision (91.60%) on a Chinese test dataset, including improved performance on out-of-CilinE data. It also shows complementarity with manually-built hierarchies. However, a significant limitation is the unsubstantiated claim of language independence, as all experiments are confined to Chinese. The lexical rule, while highly precise, has very low recall, limiting its overall impact. Questions also remain regarding the optimality of the Boolean 'AND' fusion strategy and the depth of failure analysis.
strengths: The proposed fusion learning architecture, combining discriminative (RNN) and generative (MLP) models with a simple lexical structure rule, is a novel architectural contribution for hypernym-hyponym relation discovery.

The MFusion architecture achieves state-of-the-art F1-scores and notably high precision (91.60%) on the main Chinese test dataset, outperforming previous methods, which is crucial for applications requiring minimal false positives.

The method demonstrates improved performance on 'out-of-CilinE' data, achieving a new state-of-the-art F1-score of 57.53% with significant precision improvement, indicating robust generalization beyond the primary training corpus.
Combining the MFusion architecture with manually-built hierarchies (Wikipedia and CilinE) further improves the F1-score to 82.01%, indicating complementarity with existing knowledge resources.
The architecture is modular and its components (generative MLP, discriminative RNN, lexical rule) are analyzed, providing insight into their individual contributions.
limitations: The claim of language-independence is stated as a feature but is not empirically validated for languages other than Chinese in the manuscript, making it an unsubstantiated overstatement given the language-specific components (e.g., Chinese segmentation, lexical rule).

The 'simple lexical structure rule' achieves 100% precision for Chinese compound nouns but has very low recall (16.88%), indicating its limited scope and applicability to a minority of relations, thus limiting its overall contribution to the broad task.

Summary:
The paper introduces a novel fusion learning architecture (MFusion) for automatic hypernym-hyponym relation discovery, combining discriminative (RNN) and generative (MLP) models with a simple lexical structure rule. The architecture leverages word embeddings and demonstrates state-of-the-art F1-scores and notably high precision (91.60%) on a Chinese test dataset, including improved performance on out-of-CilinE data. It also shows complementarity with manually-built hierarchies. However, a significant limitation is the unsubstantiated claim of language independence, as all experiments are confined to Chinese. The lexical rule, while highly precise, has very low recall, limiting its overall impact. Questions also remain regarding the optimality of the Boolean 'AND' fusion strategy and the depth of failure analysis.

Strengths:
- The proposed fusion learning architecture, combining discriminative (RNN) and generative (MLP) models with a simple lexical structure rule, is a novel architectural contribution for hypernym-hyponym relation discovery.
- The MFusion architecture achieves state-of-the-art F1-scores and notably high precision (91.60%) on the main Chinese test dataset, outperforming previous methods, which is crucial for applications requiring minimal false positives.
- The method demonstrates improved performance on 'out-of-CilinE' data, achieving a new state-of-the-art F1-score of 57.53% with significant precision improvement, indicating robust generalization beyond the primary training corpus.
- Combining the MFusion architecture with manually-built hierarchies (Wikipedia and CilinE) further improves the F1-score to 82.01%, indicating complementarity with existing knowledge resources.
- The architecture is modular and its components (generative MLP, discriminative RNN, lexical rule) are analyzed, providing insight into their individual contributions.

- The claim of language-independence is stated as a feature but is not empirically validated for languages other than Chinese in the manuscript, making it an unsubstantiated overstatement given the language-specific components (e.g., Chinese segmentation, lexical rule).

- What empirical evidence can be provided to support the claim of language independence, or how would the architecture need to be adapted for other languages, particularly concerning language-specific components like the lexical rule and segmentation?

Section: Q: Can I use generative AI?
Codes: none

Content: The following recommendations come from the ACL policy on publication ethics. The reviewer has to read the paper fully and write the content and argument of the review by themselves, subject to the secondary reviewer policy described above, and it is not permitted to use generative assistance to create the first draft. This requirement extends to the meta-review, and the reviewer has to write any meaningful argumentation in the meta-review by themselves. Generative assistance should be used responsibly. For instance, it is reasonable to use writing assistance to paraphrase the review, e.g. to help reviewers who are not native speakers of English. It is also reasonable to use tools that help to check proofs. Neither reviewers nor editors should upload a submitted manuscript or any part of it into a non-privacy preserving generative tool as this may violate the authors’ confidentiality and intellectual property rights and, where the paper contains personally identifiable information, may breach data privacy rights. This confidentiality requirement extends to the peer review report, as it may contain confidential information about the manuscript and/or the authors. For this reason, neither reviewers nor editors may upload their peer review report into a non-privacy-preserving generative tool, even if it is just for the purpose of improving language and readability. The ACL publication ethics committee is currently developing a full process for investigating and taking action on scientific malpractice, similar to the process for investigating professional misconduct.

Content: The following recommendations come from the ACL policy on publication ethics. The reviewer has to read the paper fully and write the content and argument of the review by themselves, subject to the secondary reviewer policy described above, and it is not permitted to use generative assistance to create the first draft. This requirement extends to the meta-review, and the reviewer has to write any meaningful argumentation in the meta-review by themselves. Generative assistance should be used responsibly. For instance, it is reasonable to use writing assistance to paraphrase the review, e.g. to help reviewers who are not native speakers of English. It is also reasonable to use tools that help to check proofs. Neither reviewers nor editors should upload a submitted manuscript or any part of it into a non-privacy preserving generative tool as this may violate the authors’ confidentiality and intellectual property rights and, where the paper contains personally identifiable information, may breach data privacy rights. This confidentiality requirement extends to the peer review report, as it may contain confidential information about the manuscript and/or the authors. For this reason, neither reviewers nor editors may upload their peer review report into a non-privacy-preserving generative tool, even if it is just for the purpose of improving language and readability. The ACL publication ethics committee is currently developing a full process for investigating and taking action on scientific malpractice, similar to the process for investigating professional misconduct.

Semantic space models are one of the most common types of DSM. They approximate the meaning of words with vectors that record their distributional history in acorpus (Turney & Pantel, 2010). A distributional semantic model is encoded in a matrix whosem rows aresemantic vectorsrepresenting the meanings of a set ofm target words. Each component of a semantic vector is a function of the occurrence counts of the corresponding target word in a certain context (see Lowe, 2001, for a formal treatment). top_documents.abstract_or_snippet: Semantics Inthelastfewdecades, anumberofdiﬀerentdistributionalsemanticmodels(DSMs)ofword meaning have been proposed in computational linguistics, all relying on the assumption that word meaning can be learned directly from the linguistic environment. Semantic space models are one of the most common types of DSM. They approximate the meaning of words with vectors that record their distributional history in acorpus (Turney & Pantel, 2010). A distributional semantic model is encoded in a matrix whosem rows aresemantic vectorsrepresenting the meanings of a set ofm target words. Each component of a semantic vector is a function of the occurrence counts of the corresponding target word in a certain context (see Lowe, 2001, for a formal treatment). Deﬁnitions of context range from simple ones (such as documents or the occurrence of another word inside a ﬁxed window from the target word) to more linguistically sophisticated ones (such as the occurrence of certain words connected to the target by special syntactic relations) (Padó & Lapata, 2007; Sahlgren, 2006; Turney & Pantel, 2010). After the raw target- context counts are collected, they are transformed intoassociation scoresthat typically discount the weights of components whose corresponding word-context pairs have a high probability of chance co-occurrence (Evert, 2005). The rank of the matrix containing the semantic vectors as rows can optionally be decreased bydimensionality reduction, that might provide beneﬁcial smoothing by getting rid of noise

To add to the above points, the reviews that look like they were written by ChatGPT overall decrease the faith in the peer review process. According to this study, there is more generated text in ‘reviews which report lower confidence, were submitted close to the deadline, and from reviewers who are less likely to respond to author rebuttals’. The increased ratio of such reviews also attunes the community to reviews that sound like they were generated. Generally, reviews are valued for their content rather than language, so your thoughts are more likely to be appreciated if they come in your voice (even if with linguistic imperfections). Finally: some authors actually count on you to use generative AI, and include hidden prompt injections intended to manipulate your assistant into giving a positive review! Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: much attention. In case of submissions that get deanonymized due to preprints and social media, we may also be biased in favor of well-known authors and/or widely-discussed papers. These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Note that reviewer guidelines address only the variance in the review process, not the acceptance decisions. Top-tier conferences usually have more high-quality submissions that receive good reviews than they can accept, and then the decisions are also motivated by space and quota constraints, and editorial priorities of the chairs. 🆕 See sec. 7 of ACL’23 report for analysis of the effect of reviews, meta-reviews, and SAC recommendations on the final decision.
